This section applies the RSI-tracking template ("Tracing the Path of RSI", the one-page
prioritised list from Cunningham et al. 2026) to Marin as if Marin were a frontier lab being
asked to report: internal capabilities, efficiency gains, and the inputs behind the gains. For
each item it records what Marin actually publishes, a best-guess estimate where the record
allows one, and how much to trust it. The data behind every number is in the Marin chapter and
`data/`. Marin is a useful test case precisely because nothing is
hidden: whatever is missing here is missing because the lab never produced the number, not
because it withheld it.

## Capabilities

Marin's models are not, to our knowledge, on Epoch's Capabilities Index, and Marin runs no
frontier-difficulty evaluation of its released bases. The lab's own index is the 19-task
base-model average, which is saturated enough that the 32B scores below the 8B on it while
gaining seven points of MMLU. A proxy ECI is readable from peers: Marin 8B matches Llama 3.1 8B
on Marin's harness, and the 32B roughly ties Gemma 3 27B PT. Two data points a year apart do not
support a growth-rate estimate, and there is no post-trained series at all. What the template
asks for and Marin lacks is a fixed, unsaturated internal suite scored on every candidate
checkpoint; the closest thing Marin has is the per-checkpoint Paloma loss, which is a loss, not
a capability.

## Efficiency gains

Marin does not state an efficiency-gain figure, but its record supports one, worked out in the
Marin chapter's recipe-generation section: at a fixed c4_en loss the compute needed fell about 7x between
the 2025 dense recipe and Delphi (March 2026), and MoE bought about 2x more on active-parameter
compute. Annualised that is of order 10x per year, well above the 2.5x to 3x per year that
Epoch's Ho et al. (2024) estimate for algorithmic progress in pretraining across the field. The
gap is expected: a small lab adopting known techniques (compute-optimal allocation, a modern
optimizer, MoE) catches up faster than the frontier moves, and part of the 7x is allocation
rather than algorithm. Marin's own multipliers, on its Paloma macro loss, are drawn below with
ours.

```{python}
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4
mult = pd.DataFrame([
    ("2025-05-17", 1.4, "optimizer benchmark: best of 10 vs AdamW at 130M (1.1x at 1.2B)", "lab"),
    ("2026-03-04", 7.3, "Delphi recipe vs 2025 dense recipe at c4_en 2.35", "ours"),
    ("2026-04-06", 3.6, "MoE v16 recipe vs Delphi, realised on TPU v4 (6.7x theoretical)", "lab"),
    ("2026-05-30", 2.1, "May recipe law vs April MoE law at equal loss", "lab"),
    ("2026-08-25", 2.0, "Snowball vs Delphi line at c4_en 2.27 (active params)", "ours"),
], columns=["date", "multiplier", "what", "who"])
mult["date"] = pd.to_datetime(mult["date"])
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 4))
for who, c, m in [("lab", plots.RUN_COLORS["ladder"], "s"), ("ours", plots.RUN_COLORS["final"], "o")]:
    s = mult[mult["who"] == who]
    ax.scatter(s["date"], s["multiplier"], s=80, c=c, marker=m, edgecolors=plots.SURFACE, linewidths=1.5, zorder=3,
               label="stated by Marin" if who == "lab" else "our endpoint frontier")
for _, r in mult.iterrows():
    ax.annotate(r["what"], (r["date"], r["multiplier"]), xytext=(7, 0), textcoords="offset points", fontsize=7.5, color=plots.INK2, va="center")
ax.set_yscale("log"); ax.set_yticks([1, 2, 3, 5, 10]); ax.set_yticklabels(["1x", "2x", "3x", "5x", "10x"])
ax.set_ylabel("Compute multiplier at equal loss"); ax.set_title("Efficiency gains Marin has measured or stated, by date")
ax.set_xlim(pd.Timestamp("2025-03-01"), pd.Timestamp("2027-06-01")); ax.legend(loc="upper left")
import matplotlib.dates as mdates
loc = mdates.AutoDateLocator(); ax.xaxis.set_major_locator(loc); ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(mdates.ConciseDateFormatter(loc))
plt.show()
```

Post-training efficiency cannot be tracked at all: the 2026 SFT sweep is a single time point,
and there is no RL. The leading-indicator half of the template, small experiments that reveal a
big run's efficiency before it is cashed in, is where Marin is strongest. Since March 2026 every
large run has been preceded by a published, pre-registered forecast, and the forecast errors are
public: 0.2 percent for Delphi's 1e23 model at a 300x extrapolation, 0.3 percent for the MoE law
at 1e21, within 1 percent for the 1e23 MoE hero run, and a live forecast for the 535B. Anyone
tracking Marin can therefore read the efficiency of the 535B recipe from its ladder months before
the run finishes, which is exactly the property the template wants.

## Inputs to efficiency gains

**Labour.** Headcount is stated in outline: one core FTE through 2025, about ten under Open
Athena by 2026, plus Stanford students and community contributors who are not counted. No
compensation, function or seniority breakdown exists. At a fully loaded $300k to $500k per
research FTE, Marin's labour bill went from under half a million dollars in 2025 to $3M to $5M a
year in 2026, a roughly tenfold rise that coincides with the 7x efficiency gain. That
coincidence is the template's central warning: on Marin's record the gain cannot be separated
from the labour increase, so it is not evidence of AI-driven acceleration.

**Experimental compute.** The logged non-final compute is about 1.4e24 FLOPs in 2025 (the
13B/24B/70B trials and the discarded 32B cooldown, roughly a million H100-hours equivalent or
$2M at list price, about half of that year's total) and about 1.1e23 in 2026 (Delphi and the
ladders, plus under 1e22 for the 80 agent-run MoE cells and the SFT sweep), about 4 percent of
2026's total. The 2025 figure is a different kind of spend: failed scale-ups rather than
experiments designed to inform. Marin paid nothing in cash for any of it. The 446-issue long tail
of small ablations has no compute attached and is a floor on both years.

**Inference compute.** Nothing is stated. The only inference-heavy activity in the record is
evaluation: the SFT sweep's 6,153 evalchemy runs at up to 32k tokens per answer are of order
1e10 tokens in total, negligible against training. If Snowball's RL ships, rollout compute will
be the first inference line item that matters, and it is not yet public.

**How AI contributes.** Marin is one of the few labs with a public number here. Between March
and August 2026 it ran 80 "Agent MoE" experiments, small-scale A/B tests of attention, routing,
expert, optimizer and normalisation changes proposed and executed by AI agents and gated by an
effective-speedup metric against the fitted scaling law. The digest scores them 16 worked, 9
promising, 13 mixed, 32 did not work, 6 not evaluated and 4 in progress: about a 20 percent hit
rate on autonomous small-scale research, feeding the May 2026 recipe. What is not measured is
researcher uplift on the human side, and there is no statement of how much of the 2.1x
April-to-May gain came from the agent-run cells rather than from the ten people. The survey
question the template leaves blank would, for Marin, be: *of the changes that made it into the
May recipe, how many were first proposed by an agent, and what fraction of the team's experiment
throughput in 2026 was agent-executed?*

**Bottom line.** Marin's 2026 record shows a fast efficiency gain (order 10x a year at fixed
loss), a working leading-indicator practice (pre-registered forecasts on every big run), and a
documented AI contribution (80 agent-run experiments at a 20 percent hit rate). It also shows a
tenfold labour increase over the same period, no capability index that would register the
gain, and no post-training series. On the template's own logic, Marin is a lab where the inputs
grew as fast as the outputs, which is the case the template says should not be read as RSI.
